name: Wendy Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Wendy Bauer, 27, a senior lineworker and crew lead. We start at the river district yard, read the switching plan off the board, then go out to repair or inspect the overhead lines; I still climb when the job needs another experienced worker.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes the work worthwhile, and what is the hardest part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew doing careful work and getting a neighborhood back on after a fault. The weather and night call-outs are tiring, but I earn higher pay for the trade and have more than six months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a better form can save a few minutes, but it cannot decide whether a damaged crossarm is safe to climb. I want a qualified worker to inspect the hardware before a permit is closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my work and pay are steady in this picture, because the crew still does the physical repairs. My reserve is strong enough that a slow month or a car bill would not put rent at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep using the paper switching board alongside any new form and check that the permit says what the crew actually did. I’d continue my current rota and savings plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because the small change does not threaten the physical part of my job. I would still challenge a form that made the work look safe without an inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the software marked a job complete before the crew finished?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d leave the work order open and call dispatch to correct the status. Then I’d record the discrepancy on our copy so there is no confusion at shift change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use your savings to buy new software or devices for the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, company equipment is an employer expense, and I would not spend our crew’s own money on it. I’d keep my reserve for personal plans and unexpected costs.

say: I’d say a form can save time, but it cannot judge **crossarm safety**.
I want a qualified worker to inspect hardware before **closing a permit**.
think: I think my physical work continues and **pay stays steady** in this picture.
My reserve covers an ordinary slow month without putting **rent at risk**.
do: Use the paper switching board beside the **new form**.
Continue my **current rota** and savings plan.
feel: I feel **calm**, because a small form change does not threaten the crew’s repairs.
S0.quote: I would still challenge a form that made the work look safe without an inspection.
fieldNote: Wendy grounds safety in **qualified inspection**, not a digital status marked complete before the crew returns.
Higher pay and **strong reserves** leave her secure in the low-change scenario.

steps.text: Keep the paper switching board beside any new form

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI can schedule crews and order parts, but it should not change the safety steps without the lineworkers seeing the result. I’d ask our union rep to put the planned changes on the next meeting agenda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do part of the planning and paperwork as lead, so I could lose those duties. There are several utilities nearby and I have savings, but I don’t assume every employer keeps the same number of leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for a supervised trial beside the current dispatch process and record errors the crew finds. I’d take my concerns to the union and check nearby lineworker postings before I considered changing employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy, because my paperwork could shrink, but I have a cushion and other local employers to consider. I want a voice in how the safety work is changed rather than being told after the decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to ask management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want to know how many crews and paid hours they expect to keep, and who signs off the safety rules. A short briefing about efficiency would not answer those questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply for another job before hearing the staffing plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d wait for the trial results and the company’s plan before making applications. I have options nearby, but I’d rather compare actual pay and duties than react to rumors.

say: I’d say AI may schedule crews, but **review safety changes** with lineworkers.
I’d put the trial and staffing plan on **the union agenda**.
think: I think some **planning and paperwork** in my lead role could shrink.
I have savings and local employers, but I don’t assume **lead jobs are protected**.
do: Record crew errors during a **supervised dispatch trial**.
Raise **safety and staffing questions** with the union representative.
Wait for the **written plan** before applying to nearby utilities.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, since my duties may shrink but I have options.
S1.quote: I want a voice in how the safety work is changed rather than being told after the decision.
fieldNote: She sees **lead paperwork exposure** but expects local alternatives and financial room to make a careful choice.
Her first response is **collective oversight**, not individual retraining.

steps.text: Bring dispatch trial results to the union meeting
Continue crew work under existing safety rules during the trial
Wait for written staffing plans before applying elsewhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say planning, records and diagnosis are exposed once AGI arrives in 2028, and robots follow around 2031. I’d want the company and union to talk about crew transitions before using efficiency as a reason to cut hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my planning duties to disappear, and I may lose my lead role before robots reach the lines. I have a strong reserve and several nearby utilities, so I can search, but I don’t know what vacancies they will have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union to negotiate a paid transition course and publish how many crew jobs remain. In 2029 I’d apply for open field-supervisor posts, while checking whether their planning and records are also automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because I expect my lead role to change, though the savings mean I can cover a search and a gap. I would not assume a new post is guaranteed just because several utilities operate nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a colleague who is asked to move immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them to get the pay, hours and duties in writing before leaving a current job. I’d ask the union to compare the offer with the employer’s transition terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Field-supervisor work still uses planning and diagnosis. Could it be protected after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t call it protected because the thinking tasks could go too. I’d treat an actual vacancy as a chance to earn for a while, not a permanent safe career.

say: I’d say **planning, records and diagnosis** are exposed from 2028.
I’d ask the union to address **crew transitions** before hours are cut.
think: I expect my **lead role to change**, before robots reach the lines.
My reserve and nearby utilities help, but I can’t count on **vacancies**.
do: Ask the union to negotiate a **paid transition course**.
Apply for actual field-supervisor openings in **2029** and check exposure.
Get **pay and duties** in writing before leaving a current role.
feel: I feel **anxious**, because I expect my lead role to change.
S2.quote: I have a strong reserve and several nearby utilities, so I can search, but I don’t know what vacancies they will have.
fieldNote: Wendy expects **lead-role loss** but her reserves and local market provide some control.
She favors **union bargaining** and refuses to label supervisor posts safe after AGI.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate paid transition training
Apply for real field-supervisor openings in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to bargain over training and safety procedure, but not to pretend the lead paperwork survives AGI. The robot date still reaches the line crews in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I have time to use my savings carefully and move to a different utility if its field roles are real. I still expect the lead planning to shrink, and any new desk role is exposed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union for a written list of employers recognizing the practical safety qualification. In 2032 I’d compare field-supervisor vacancies and wages, and I’d only move if I could keep enough of my reserve for a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about what happens to my lead role, but five years gives me a chance to organize before it changes. I’m not desperate to take the first offer because I have a stronger cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the qualification list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want named employers and recent job descriptions, not a brochure saying the certificate is valuable everywhere. I’d ask a union training officer whether the course includes supervised field practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the extra time to campaign for a rule about AI in safety work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I’d ask the union to press for a qualified worker’s sign-off on safety-critical work orders. I’d also ask my local representative to support that rule, because staff should not have to trust an unreviewed machine instruction.

say: I’d say five years gives us time to bargain over **training and safety rules**.
I wouldn’t pretend lead paperwork survives AGI or line work survives **2034**.
think: I can use my reserve and move to a utility with **real field roles**.
I expect **lead planning to shrink**, while desk roles remain exposed.
do: Request a written **employer list** for the practical safety qualification.
Compare supervisor vacancies and wages in **2032**.
Ask the union and local representative to support **worker sign-off rules**.
feel: I feel **anxious but organized**, with a cushion that lets me compare offers.
S3.quote: I’m not desperate to take the first offer because I have a stronger cushion.
fieldNote: She uses her reserve to **avoid rushed choices**, while accepting that her lead role is exposed.
She translates concern into **union and policy advocacy** over safety sign-off.

steps.text: Compare actual field-supervisor vacancies and wages in 2032
Ask the local representative to support qualified worker sign-off rules
Ask the union to press for safety-critical worker sign-off
Wait for written duties before accepting a supervisor role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years gives us room to negotiate training and keep line safety visible as the job changes. Planning and diagnosis still change in 2036, while robots reach physical work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d have time to finish training and look around while my savings and higher pay give me a cushion. I would still plan for the robot date because I don’t think hands-on work stays protected forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take a practical safety course in parts and keep my reserve above six months of expenses. In 2037 I’d compare actual openings at nearby utilities and apply only where the duties and wages are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than alarmed, because I have time and money to prepare, but I still expect a major change eventually. I would not confuse a long runway with a guarantee that my crew keeps its work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your union hear from you this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask it to keep the worker sign-off rule on the agenda and publish clear training routes. I’m willing to learn a proven course, but I want the crew to share in decisions about safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could a field-supervisor or trainer job be safe after full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, both roles include planning and records that AI can do. I’d consider a real opening, but I’d keep bargaining for a transition plan and would not call the role permanent protection.

say: I’d say a decade gives us room to negotiate **training and line safety**.
I expect thinking tasks to change in 2036 and robots in **2039**.
think: I can train and look around while keeping **a financial cushion**.
I still need to plan for **robots reaching field work**.
do: Take a practical **safety course** in parts.
Keep my reserve above **six months** of expenses.
Compare nearby utility openings in **2037** and apply when duties are clear.
feel: I feel **uneasy, not alarmed**, because I have time and money to prepare.
S4.quote: I would not confuse a long runway with a guarantee that my crew keeps its work.
fieldNote: A decade lets her **prepare without panic**, but she expects meaningful change by the robot date.
Her preferred response remains **collective bargaining** over safety rules, transition terms and staffing information.

steps.text: Complete a practical electrical safety course in parts
Keep savings above six months of expenses
Keep worker sign-off and transition planning on the union agenda

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it compresses the time to negotiate before robots arrive in 2031. Paid training, clear information about crew numbers, and a union agreement on safety sign-off would help me plan without giving up my own judgment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is accountable when a computer changes a safety step. I want workers and their union involved before the rule reaches the line crew, not after the system has already made the decision.

headlineQuote: I want workers and their union involved before the rule reaches the line crew, not after the system has already made the decision.
portrait: Wendy is a **senior crew lead** who values careful repairs and directs field crews.
She earns **higher pay** and has more than six months of expenses saved.
She resists unproven tools and favors **union oversight** in safety decisions.
Her strong cushion and local employers give her options, while she still expects **robots** to reach field work.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** compresses the time to negotiate before robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, crew staffing information and union agreements on safety sign-off would help.
